texts.orig: Q: What growth rates do investors expect at each stage of the business?
texts.text: Q: What growth rates do investors expect at each stage of the business?

texts.label: text
texts.orig: To get you a clear answer, I reached out to two dozen of the smartest investors I know and asked them what they consider GOOD and GREAT growth rate by stage of business. Below is what I learned.
texts.text: To get you a clear answer, I reached out to two dozen of the smartest investors I know and asked them what they consider GOOD and GREAT growth rate by stage of business. Below is what I learned.

texts.orig: 1. In the early stages, investors don’t care about month-over-month growth
texts.text: 1. In the early stages, investors don’t care about month-over-month growth

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Why? Because percentages with a small base don’t mean much. This sentiment was true across every investor I talked to, e.g.:
texts.text: Why? Because percentages with a small base don’t mean much. This sentiment was true across every investor I talked to, e.g.:

texts.label: text
texts.orig: “I look at MoM only really as a proxy for how fast it ramps to $1m ARR.
texts.text: “I look at MoM only really as a proxy for how fast it ramps to $1m ARR.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: We don’t anchor on the specific percentages for MoM growth because the percentage represents a pretty small dollar difference with small denominators. For example, 10% vs. 20% growth at $100K ARR isn’t substantial. Every percentage means different things in an absolute sense when the denominator is small.
texts.text: We don’t anchor on the specific percentages for MoM growth because the percentage represents a pretty small dollar difference with small denominators. For example, 10% vs. 20% growth at $100K ARR isn’t substantial. Every percentage means different things in an absolute sense when the denominator is small.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Another way of thinking about it through a MoM lens is that we’d want to see accelerating MoM growth (it going from 10% to 12% to 15%, for instance) to see that the company is picking up momentum.”
texts.text: Another way of thinking about it through a MoM lens is that we’d want to see accelerating MoM growth (it going from 10% to 12% to 15%, for instance) to see that the company is picking up momentum.”

texts.label: text
texts.orig: That being said, if you’re looking for a month-over-month benchmark below $1m ARR, answers typically fell in the 15%-25% range.
texts.text: That being said, if you’re looking for a month-over-month benchmark below $1m ARR, answers typically fell in the 15%-25% range.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: for early-stage B2B businesses, investors focus on how quickly they ramp to $1m ARR after going live
texts.text: for early-stage B2B businesses, investors focus on how quickly they ramp to $1m ARR after going live

texts.label: text
texts.orig: As John Luttig (Founders Fund) put it:
texts.text: As John Luttig (Founders Fund) put it:

texts.label: text
texts.orig: “In the early stages it’s mostly about time from launch to your current ARR.
texts.text: “In the early stages it’s mostly about time from launch to your current ARR.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: If you grew to $500k ARR in 3mo post-launch, that’s more impressive than $1m in 24mo post-launch. Generally, 0 to $1m ARR in 12mo or shorter is great. There are obvious exceptions to this—not every company’s success can be measured in ARR since launch (Figma, OSS, etc.).”
texts.text: If you grew to $500k ARR in 3mo post-launch, that’s more impressive than $1m in 24mo post-launch. Generally, 0 to $1m ARR in 12mo or shorter is great. There are obvious exceptions to this—not every company’s success can be measured in ARR since launch (Figma, OSS, etc.).”

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Broadly, the expectation is that getting to $1m ARR within a year of launch is GOOD, and getting there in three quarters (9 months) is GREAT.
texts.text: Broadly, the expectation is that getting to $1m ARR within a year of launch is GOOD, and getting there in three quarters (9 months) is GREAT.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: “Velocity is everything post-launch. As the company matures, it’s less about convincing investors to dream the dream and more about proving the dream is real, executable, and monetizable.”

texts.label: text
texts.orig: For this reason, you want to be strategic about when you launch:

texts.label: text
texts.orig: “If you’ve launched and have very little traction, it’s worse than being pre-launch, because it shows the market/value prop is already demonstrably weak. This is why no data is better than bad/small data.”

texts.label: text
texts.orig: However, a couple of investors specifically said that they don’t care about how long it takes you to get going, as long as when you do get going, it really gets going:
texts.text: However, a couple of investors specifically said that they don’t care about how long it takes you to get going, as long as when you do get going, it really gets going:

texts.label: text
texts.orig: “We’re less concerned about ramp to $1mm of ARR, or growth rates every year after launch. Some of our biggest winners took several years to really get going and find strong PMF. But once they do, we want them to take off. In other words, if a business grew revenues from $500k > $5mm this year, I wouldn’t care whether it was launched 1 or 5 years ago.”
texts.text: “We’re less concerned about ramp to $1mm of ARR, or growth rates every year after launch. Some of our biggest winners took several years to really get going and find strong PMF. But once they do, we want them to take off. In other words, if a business grew revenues from $500k > $5mm this year, I wouldn’t care whether it was launched 1 or 5 years ago.”

texts.label: text
texts.orig: And if you get out of the gate slowly, you can sometimes still catch up:
texts.text: And if you get out of the gate slowly, you can sometimes still catch up:

texts.label: text
texts.orig: “Investors tend to prize early velocity. This makes sense: it increases the likelihood that you will compound to very high revenues. But speed of 0 to $1M of ARR has, in my experience, been less predictive than speed from $500K to $5M ARR. The latter is indicative of having ‘minimum viable durability’ of your revenue, which will compound over a longer period. Oftentimes, during the 0 to $1M phase, a company is still working to optimize retention, experimenting with efficiency, and initially segmenting their customers.”
texts.text: “Investors tend to prize early velocity. This makes sense: it increases the likelihood that you will compound to very high revenues. But speed of 0 to $1M of ARR has, in my experience, been less predictive than speed from $500K to $5M ARR. The latter is indicative of having ‘minimum viable durability’ of your revenue, which will compound over a longer period. Oftentimes, during the 0 to $1M phase, a company is still working to optimize retention, experimenting with efficiency, and initially segmenting their customers.”

texts.orig: 3. If you don’t have strong immediate ARR growth, you can show success in other ways
texts.text: 3. If you don’t have strong immediate ARR growth, you can show success in other ways

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Without fast ARR growth, you’ll need to show strong signals that people really want your product—through high retention and efficiency:
texts.text: Without fast ARR growth, you’ll need to show strong signals that people really want your product—through high retention and efficiency:

texts.label: text
texts.orig: “Revenue growth is really an output for what else is happening in the business—basically how much customers love the product and how efficient it is to get more of them. Cohorted revenue retention and/or purchase behavior (ideally U-shaped cohorts where net revenue retention goes up over a year) and marketing spend/revenue (efficiency) are the most important factors to the health and velocity of a business.”
texts.text: “Revenue growth is really an output for what else is happening in the business—basically how much customers love the product and how efficient it is to get more of them. Cohorted revenue retention and/or purchase behavior (ideally U-shaped cohorts where net revenue retention goes up over a year) and marketing spend/revenue (efficiency) are the most important factors to the health and velocity of a business.”

texts.label: text
texts.orig: “The key thing is that there’s some leading indicator of ARR that is intrinsically compounding at a high rate. It’s often early users with taste representative of future users loving something. For example, if the business is going to be sales-led, are our salespeople incredibly productive (or do I think they will be)? Are sales cycles oddly short, do customers rave about us and tell their friends (typically leading to oddly low CAC), etc.?”

texts.label: text
texts.orig: And Ellen Chisa (Boldstart) reminds us that in the early days, it’s often a trap to focus too much on growth:
texts.text: And Ellen Chisa (Boldstart) reminds us that in the early days, it’s often a trap to focus too much on growth:

texts.label: text
texts.orig: “It’s a huge mistake to focus on the growth number before getting retention. You can often hit the ‘great’ number at an early stage by brute force because the numbers are so small. Unfortunately, that won’t translate to continued growth, and then you’ll end up in a worse place than if you’d spent longer to hit the fundamentals.”

texts.orig: Grew quickly out of the gate and maintained that growth rate: Instagram, Twitter, Dropbox, etc. Within months of launch crossed 1M users, then got to 10M within the next year or two, then got to 100M within the next year or two (I’m not sure those numbers are exactly right for those companies, but directionally correct).
texts.text: Grew quickly out of the gate and maintained that growth rate: Instagram, Twitter, Dropbox, etc. Within months of launch crossed 1M users, then got to 10M within the next year or two, then got to 100M within the next year or two (I’m not sure those numbers are exactly right for those companies, but directionally correct).

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Uber, Gmail, RecRoom: started out good, but hit key unlocks along the way, so their growth curves look more like step functions. Uber’s was UberX, RecRoom’s was the introduction of the Oculus platform, Gmail was enough machines/leaving invite-only. E.g. it took Gmail roughly 3 years to get to 20M users, then about 4 more years to get to 200M, then crossed 1B and 2B (I think) mostly because of bundling with Android.
